query: For high-entropy alloys, what testable mechanistic hypothesis could explain what governs hardness and strength and why? Define a controlled comparison that would reveal the governing behavior, predict the observations relative to a baseline, state the limits within which the hypothesis should hold, identify evidence that would support it, and specify an observation that would falsify it.

generation.hypothesis: Within single-phase FCC high-entropy alloys (HEAs), room-temperature hardness (HV) and 0.2 % offset yield strength (σ0.2) increase approximately linearly with the magnitude of atomic-size lattice distortion (quantified by the atomic size variance parameter δ); i.e. ΔHV ≈ +10 ± 4 kg mm⁻² and Δσ0.2 ≈ +35 ± 15 MPa per 1 % increase in δ up to δ ≈ 6 %.
generation.material_initial_state: Equiatomic or near-equiatomic single-phase FCC HEAs derived from the Cantor alloy family (e.g., CoCrFeMnNi) with recrystallized, equiaxed grains >10 µm and negligible texture.
generation.intervention: Systematically substitute a large-radius element (e.g., Al or Ti) for an isovalent base element to create a compositional series that alters δ from ≈0 % to ≈6 % while maintaining the FCC phase and identical average valence-electron concentration.
generation.conditions: Room temperature mechanical testing; strain rate 10⁻³ s⁻¹; no prior cold work; ambient atmosphere.
generation.structural_mediator: Magnitude of local lattice distortion around each solute atom, quantified by δ = √(Σ c_i (1 - r_i / r̄)²) × 100 %, where r_i is the atomic radius of element i and r̄ is the radius averaged over all elements.
generation.mechanism: Greater lattice distortion raises the elastic interaction energy between edge dislocations and the local strain fields, thereby increasing the critical resolved shear stress needed for dislocation glide (solid-solution strengthening).
generation.predicted_outcome: Alloys with higher δ will display proportionally higher hardness and yield strength relative to the baseline Cantor alloy; e.g. raising δ from 0.3 % (CoCrFeMnNi) to 3 % (Al0.3CoCrFeMnNi) should raise hardness from ≈180 HV to ≈210 HV and σ0.2 from ≈420 MPa to ≈525 MPa.
generation.baseline: CoCrFeMnNi (δ ≈ 0.3 %): HV ≈ 180 ± 10 kg mm⁻², σ0.2 ≈ 420 ± 20 MPa under the stated conditions.
generation.boundary: Hypothesis expected to hold for: (a) single-phase FCC HEAs with 0 % < δ < 6 %, (b) grain sizes >10 µm (to minimize Hall-Petch effects), (c) temperatures below 0.3 Tm (to suppress diffusion-controlled mechanisms), and (d) alloys free of second-phase precipitates or significant chemical short-range order.
generation.uncertainty: Slope of strengthening vs. δ may vary with elastic modulus mismatch and any incipient short-range ordering; beyond δ ≈ 6 % second-phase formation may dominate, invalidating the linear relationship.

falsification_experiment.design: Synthesize a five-alloy series CoCrFeMnNiAlx with x = 0, 0.1, 0.2, 0.3, 0.4 (mol fraction) by arc-melting and homogenization. Confirm single FCC phase by XRD and EBSD; adjust heat treatment to obtain identical grain sizes (~20 µm). Measure δ from composition, verify local distortion by XRD peak broadening (Williamson–Hall) or synchrotron PDF. Perform Vickers hardness tests (500 g load, 15 s dwell) and uniaxial compression tests.
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If hardness and σ0.2 do not increase monotonically with δ—or the slope is statistically indistinguishable from zero (p > 0.05) within δ ≤ 6 %—the hypothesis is falsified.
